title: The 12-bar blues, the shuffle and first licks
summary: The twelve-bar pattern under thousands of songs, the swung shuffle feel, and your first real blues licks with the blue note.
intro: The 12-bar blues is a chord pattern twelve bars long: four bars on chord I, two on IV, two back on I, then one each of V, IV, I and I (or V to turn round). In E that's E, A and B. Once your ears know it, you can follow most blues and early rock songs the first time you hear them.
The shuffle is the feel. Beats split long-short instead of evenly, like a heartbeat: da-dum, da-dum. The rhythm items here are all in that feel, so let it sink in.

Then the licks. Blues licks are short phrases from the minor pentatonic box, often with one extra note: the flat fifth, called the blue note. Add it to box 1 and you have the blues scale. Learn a few licks exactly as recorded, then use them in your own jams.
tips: Count the bars out loud the first few times: one, two, three, four, then the change. The 12-bar comes round so often that you'll soon feel the changes coming.
Shuffle feel: think 'ONE-and TWO-and' with the 'and' late and short. Tap your foot on the beat, not on the 'and'.
A riff on chord I usually moves to IV as the same shape one string up, and to V two frets above that. Learn it once, move it.
The blue note is a passing note. Slide or bend through it; don't sit on it.
Steal licks. Play them exactly like the record first, then change one note or the rhythm and make them yours.
Leave space between licks. In the blues, what you don't play counts as much as what you do.
credit: The order follows Justin Sandercoe's path (justinguitar.com): the 12-bar blues and shuffle in his beginner course, 12-bar variations, then basic blues improvisation with the minor pentatonic, then the 'five blues licks from pattern 1' idea from his Essential Blues Lead Guitar course: learn a handful of licks note for note, then use them. Freddie King's Hide Away is a classic study piece for blues players. Thanks also to the many teachers who explain the blues scale this way.

riffs.name: The 12-bar riff
riffs.title: Green Onions
riffs.about: One full 12-bar blues in F, played with one small riff that moves with the chords. It's the clearest way to hear the 12-bar: four bars on F, two on Bb, two on F, then C, Bb, F, F.
how: The riff on F: first fret of the low E string three times, then fret 4, then first fret of the A string.
On Bb, move the whole thing up one string: A string fret 1, fret 4, D string fret 1.
On C it starts on the A string at fret 3. Same shape again.
Count the bars. The change to Bb comes after four, and the C comes in bar nine.

riffs.name: The boogie riff
riffs.title: Roadhouse Blues
riffs.about: A shuffle on the open low E with a punch at the end of every bar. This is the shuffle feel at its simplest: one string, one rhythm, played until it grooves.
how: Pick the open low E in the long-short shuffle rhythm. Light palm mute.
The punch: fifth fret of the low E string, then slide it up to fret 7.
Next time round the punch is the fifth fret of the A string, also slid up to 7.
Keep the picking hand moving down-up in time even when you're not hitting the string. That keeps the swing steady.

riffs.name: The opening: lick and shuffle
riffs.title: Hide Away
riffs.about: The first four bars of a blues standard: a quick lick on the top strings, then a shuffle on the low strings, twice, then a third lick that leads to the change. Freddie King plays lead and rhythm at once, and here you do too.
how: The lick: open B string twice, hammer on to fret 2, open high E, then fret 2 on the high E, sliding up to 4. Open position, very quick.
The shuffle: the open low E together with a note on the A string, which moves between open, fret 2 and fret 4. Palm mute both strings together.
The second lick reaches fret 4 on the high E and comes back down with a pull-off.
Jump between the top and bottom strings without stopping. The lick is short; the shuffle keeps the time.

riffs.name: The answer lick
riffs.title: Boom Boom
riffs.about: Blues licks in box 1 of E minor at the twelfth fret, answering the singer. The first one walks up to the blue note; the answer that follows uses two small bends: a quarter-tone curl, then a push up a semitone to the blue note.
how: Home position: first finger at fret 12, ring finger at 14, little finger at 15.
The opening phrase is all on the G string: frets 12, 14 and 15 (the blue note), and back.
Both bends are on the G string at fret 14. The first is a tiny curl; the second goes up a semitone. Bend with the ring finger and push with the fingers behind it.
Each answer ends on the E at fret 14 of the D string. Let it ring until the singer comes back.

riffs.name: The E blues scale, box 1
riffs.title: Boom Boom
riffs.about: Box 1 of E minor pentatonic at the twelfth fret, plus the blue note in two places: fret 13 on the A string and fret 15 on the G string. Every note of the Boom Boom lick is in here. Jam over it with the lick and your own variations.

riffs.name: The first twelve bars
riffs.title: Hide Away
riffs.about: A full 12-bar blues in E, lead and shuffle together: the opening, then the same idea over A, back to E, a bar on B, a bar on A, and a turnaround. About twenty seconds and over a hundred notes, so take the wait mode slowly.
how: Bars 1 to 4 are the opening item.
On A the shuffle moves up a string: the open A with the D string at frets 0, 2, 4 and 5.
Over B (bar 9) the lick repeats one note on the high E string, fret 2, again and again. Keep it even.
The last two bars are a turnaround: G string notes bouncing off the open high E. Learn it on its own in wait mode if it trips you up.
